en: Hunters camped on the island around 10,000 BCE, but Cyprus was settled around 8800 BCE by cultivators who shipped in wheat, barley and dogs; wild boar had been introduced by earlier hunters, and cattle, sheep and goats followed by boat over the next few centuries. They built round stone houses in tight villages and made bowls from grey andesite rather than clay. There was no ruler above the village.

After the Aceramic villages emptied, the island was quiet until new farming communities appeared around 4500 BCE. They made the first Cypriot pottery, painted in the north and combed in the south, and lived in scattered villages that rarely lasted more than a few generations.

The first copper appears, hammered native metal made into small ornaments and then into hooks and chisels, and a striking figurine tradition in blue-green picrolite stone. Villages grew larger and buildings more formal, but the island was still a world of villages.

Around 2400 BCE new arrivals from Anatolia brought the cattle-drawn plough, rectangular mudbrick houses, and the island's first real copper industry; tin bronze became common only later, in the Middle Bronze Age. Copper from the Troodos foothills began to be worked in quantity, and the Red Polished pottery of this age is among the most inventive the island ever made.

By the Late Bronze Age Cyprus was Alashiya, a copper-exporting kingdom whose king addressed the pharaoh as 'my brother' in the Amarna letters. Towns had ashlar buildings, a script of their own (Cypro-Minoan) and warehouses of oxhide copper ingots. Mycenaean pottery arrived in quantity from the fourteenth century BCE, carried mostly by Cypriot and Levantine ships; Aegean settlers came only after 1200 BCE, and the collapse that ended the Bronze Age remade the island.
No king of Alashiya is known by name
The Alashiya letters never name their sender. Kinyras, the Cypriot king of the Iliad, is legend.

en: The only king of Alashiya whose name survives, from letters found at Ugarit; the kings who wrote to Egypt in the Amarna archive are all anonymous, and this attribution should be checked against a specialist edition before publication.

After 1050 BCE Greek-speakers founded new towns, and by the seventh century the island held about ten small kingdoms. They wrote Greek in the old Cypriot syllabary, and they shared the island with a Phoenician colony at Kition, settled from Tyre around 850 BCE. At the very end of this age the kings of Salamis began to be buried with horses and chariots. No one power ruled the whole island.
No Cypriot king is attested by name before 673 BCE
The earliest named kings are the ten of Esarhaddon's prism, listed under the Archaic era.

en: The Cypriot king of the Iliad, who gave Agamemnon a breastplate; a figure of myth attached to Paphos, not a historical ruler.

en: Struck the first Cypriot coins, silver with a recumbent ram and his name in the syllabary, and dedicated a censer at Delphi.
Shut out of his own city by his brother Onesilos, he fled to the Persians and was restored when the revolt collapsed.
Led the island into the Ionian Revolt, besieged loyalist Amathus, and was killed in battle; the Amathusians hung his head over their gate.
Deserted to the Persians during the decisive battle, taking his chariots with him, and handed them the war.
First of the Phoenician kings of Kition known from coins, with Herakles for Melqart on the obverse.
The last independent king of Idalion, named on the bronze tablet that hires a physician during the siege; his city fell to Kition around 450 BCE.
Struck the recumbent lion coinage of Amathus on a stubbornly local weight standard.
Seized his throne at twenty, extended his rule over most of the island, fought Persia for a decade and kept his crown as a king to a king; Isocrates wrote an encomium for him.
Set up a trophy to Baal Oz for a victory in his first year, probably over Evagoras, and struck the first gold at Kition.
Son of Evagoras; reformed the coinage on a new standard and abandoned the Cypriot syllabary on his money.
Ruled Kition, Idalion and, from 342/341 BCE, Tamassos, numbering his regnal years on his coins for more than forty-five years; Ptolemy I had him executed.
Driven out by his own people, he took service with the Persian king and tried to win the throne back with Persian help.
Sold his city and his royal title to Pumayyaton of Kition for fifty talents and grew old at Amathus on the proceeds.
Held Salamis through a Persian siege, then sent ships to Alexander at Tyre and was rewarded with Tamassos.
Alexander's man and then Ptolemy's, the last king of Salamis; his family killed themselves in the palace, and an empty mound in the necropolis is thought to be his memorial.
Moved his capital to the new harbour town of Nea Paphos and was forced by Ptolemy to take his own life.
The first Marion king to strike gold; Ptolemy arrested him for siding with Antigonus, razed his city and moved its people to Paphos.
Last king of Lapethos, deposed and arrested by Ptolemy I in the same sweep, along with the ruler of Kyrenia.
The last Amathusian king in the record; he dedicated a gold wreath to Apollo on Delos in 313 BCE.
Married Eirene, a daughter of Ptolemy I, and so outlived every other Cypriot dynasty; his gold shows Apollo and Aphrodite.
Brother of Ptolemy I, governor at Salamis and the first man to strike coin on Cyprus as an outsider rather than a king; the kingdoms were over.

Seven Cypriot kings submitted to Sargon II of Assyria around 709–707 BCE, and Esarhaddon's scribes listed ten kings of the island in 673. Egypt made Cyprus tributary under Amasis around 560 BCE, and by about 545 the Persians had taken it into their empire. Cyprus lay within a Persian province, but the city-kingdoms kept their own dynasties, coinage and quarrels.

Ekishtura of Idalion, Pilagura of Chytroi, Kisu of Salamis, Ituandar of Paphos, Eresu of Soli, Damasu of Kourion, Admesu of Tamassos, Damusi of Qart-hadasht (Kition), Unasagusu of Ledra and Bususu of Nure (Amathus?). Some identifications are debated.

en: Deserted to the Persians during the battle near Salamis, deciding it.

Cyprus lay within a Persian satrapy but the city-kingdoms retained local dynasties. Salamis under Evagoras I became a centre of Greek culture and a thorn in the Persian side, and Greek fleets came three times, in 478, around 460 and in 450, to pull the island into the Greek world. Persian control was real but never total.
Expelled the Phoenician usurper Abdemon, Hellenised Salamis, fought Persia from 391 to about 380; murdered in 374.
Son of Evagoras I; Isocrates addressed two speeches to him.
Pro-Persian; deposed by his nephew Pnytagoras, later Persian governor of Sidon.
Joined the anti-Persian revolt of the 340s, survived, then fought for Alexander at Tyre and received Tamassos.
Last king of Salamis; backed Ptolemy and became governor of the island.
Baalmilk I, Azbaal, Baalmilk II of Kition

Last king of Kition; sold Tamassos to Pnytagoras; executed by Ptolemy.
Last king of Idalion, named on the bronze Idalion Tablet.
Last king of Paphos; refounded Nea Paphos; forced to suicide by Ptolemy.
Androkles of Amathus, Pasikrates of Kourion, Stasioikos II of Marion, Stasikrates and Eunostos of Soli

en: After Alexander the city-kingdoms were abolished by Ptolemy I, and for two and a half centuries Cyprus was Egypt's timber yard, copper mine, grain store and naval base. A Ptolemaic governor ruled from Nea Paphos. Greek koine became the language of government, and the old Cypriot syllabary faded out by the end of the third century BCE.
Last king of Salamis, made Ptolemy's governor of the whole island; died by suicide or murder.
Ptolemy I's brother; governed Cyprus until Demetrius took Salamis in 306.
Earliest governor (strategos) attested by inscriptions, under Ptolemy IV; based at Salamis.
Strategos under the boy-king Ptolemy V; later chancellor in Alexandria.
Strategos who handed Cyprus to Antiochus IV in 168 and defected to the Seleucids.
Strategos and high priest of the island under Ptolemy VIII.
Younger brother of Ptolemy XII of Egypt, king of Cyprus as a separate kingdom; killed himself when Cato arrived.

Annexed in 58 BCE, Cyprus was a quiet, wealthy province of theatres, baths and villas. Paul and Barnabas preached here around 45 CE and the island claims the first Christian governor. Salamis was ruined in the Jewish revolt of 115–117, and a Christian island was already taking shape when the earthquakes of the 340s brought the ancient cities down.
Special commissioner who carried out the annexation; not a governor.
Governed Cilicia with Cyprus attached and wrote about the island's debts.
Twice proconsul of Cyprus, known from his tomb inscription at Histonium.
The proconsul who heard Paul at Paphos according to Acts 13.
Proconsul who rebuilt the Kourion theatre after an earthquake.
Proconsul named on a Kourion inscription for a statue of Nero.

Cyprus was a Christian island with an independent church from 431 CE. Arab fleets raided from 649, and from 688 to 965 the island was a strange shared possession, paying tax to both the Caliphate and Constantinople. In 965 Nikephoros II Phokas's general Niketas Chalkoutzes recovered it, Cyprus became a Byzantine theme, and inland Nicosia became the capital.
Bishop of Salamis-Constantia and metropolitan of Cyprus; heresy-hunter and author of the Panarion.
Led the Cypriot bishops at Ephesus and won canon 8, the charter of the Church's independence.
Found the relics of Barnabas and secured Zeno's confirmation of autocephaly.
Archbishop deported with his flock to Nea Justinianoupolis; source of the title the Church of Cyprus still uses.
Archbishop who resigned in protest at official abuses; later Patriarch of Constantinople.
Usurper who ruled the island as a self-styled emperor until Richard I deposed him.
Rebuilt earthquake-ruined Salamis as Constantia, remitted its taxes and made it the capital of the island.
Paid for the basilica over Barnabas's tomb and gave the archbishop the sceptre, the purple and the red ink.
Reign of the great mosaic floors and the last generation of five-aisled basilicas; Archbishop Philoxenos enlarged the Barnabas shrine under him.
Agreed the condominium with Abd al-Malik in 688, then moved much of the population to Nea Justinianoupolis near Cyzicus in 691.
Bishop who is said to have followed his captured flock to the caliph's court and brought them home.
Patrician who recovered the island for Nikephoros II Phokas with a small force and made it a theme.
Governor who rebelled, was captured and was paraded through the Hippodrome dressed as a woman.
Rebel governor put down by John Doukas and Manuel Boutoumites for Alexios I.
The island's most effective Byzantine governor, patron of the paintings at Koutsovendis and scourge of Levantine pirates.
Governor captured when Raynald of Chatillon raided the island; his defeat let the Franks plunder it for three weeks.

Richard the Lionheart took the island in 1191 and it passed to Guy de Lusignan. His dynasty ruled for three centuries, building Gothic cathedrals and castles and putting the Greek Church under a Latin archbishop. It grew rich on Famagusta's trade after Acre fell, then slowly bled to Genoese and Mamluk pressure. Cyprus was the last crusader kingdom.
Lord of Cyprus, never crowned king; former King of Jerusalem.
Guy's brother; crowned first King of Cyprus in 1197; also King of Jerusalem 1197–1205.
Son of Aimery; child king under regency.
Long minority; Ibelin regents fight Frederick II's supporters 1228–1233.
Died aged about fourteen; end of the direct male line.
Of Antioch-Lusignan; also King of Jerusalem from 1268.
Lost Acre in 1291; deposed 1306–1310 by his brother Amalric of Tyre.
Peak of prosperity; patron of Bellapais.
Crusader king; sacked Alexandria in 1365; murdered by his knights in 1369.
Held hostage in Genoa until 1385; titular King of Armenia from 1393.
Defeated and captured by the Mamluks at Khirokitia in 1426.
Queen regnant, driven out by her half-brother; died in Rome in 1487.
Seized the crown with Mamluk backing; recovered Famagusta from Genoa; married Caterina Cornaro.
Venetian-born last queen; forced to abdicate in 1489.

Venice acquired the island through Queen Caterina Cornaro and ran it as a heavily taxed colony and a forward base against the Ottomans. Its lasting legacy is stone: the star-shaped walls of Nicosia and the vast ramparts of Famagusta. Famagusta's were complete by 1562; Nicosia's were still unfinished when the Ottomans landed in 1570.

Cyprus was governed from Nicosia by a lieutenant sent out from Venice, normally for two years, advised by two counsellors, with a Capitano commanding Famagusta, rectors in the lesser towns and a Provveditore Generale sent out in emergencies.

en: First lieutenant of Cyprus, appointed in the year Caterina Cornaro abdicated.
Lieutenant of Cyprus, later Doge of Venice from 1553 to 1554.
Lieutenant of Cyprus, later second in command of the Christian fleet and mortally wounded at Lepanto in 1571.
Lieutenant during the invasion; blamed by contemporaries for a timid defence and killed when Nicosia was stormed on 9 September 1570.
Lieutenant of Cyprus, then Capitano Generale da Mar who commanded the Venetian fleet at Lepanto, and Doge from 1577 to 1578.
Last lieutenant appointed; never reached the island.
Capitano of Famagusta, who held the fortress for ten and a half months and was flayed alive on 17 August 1571 after the surrender terms were broken.
Umbrian condottiere and governor of the island's troops, who ran the fighting defence of Famagusta and was killed at the surrender.

After the sieges of 1570 and 1571 Cyprus became an Ottoman province for three centuries. Latin rule ended and the Orthodox Church was restored, its archbishop becoming the leader of the Greek community. Turkish settlers formed the island's Muslim population. Neglect, locusts and heavy taxation marked much of the period.
Commander of the conquest and the island's first governor; he had Bragadin flayed at Famagusta and gave his name to its cathedral-mosque.
First beylerbeyi of the new province of Cyprus, credited with building the Buyuk Han in Nicosia; some scholars give the han to his successor Sinan Pasha.
Cyprus was a full eyalet under a governor of pasha rank with sanjaks on the mainland; some seventy governors came and went, few staying more than two years.
The island was downgraded to a sanjak assigned to the Ottoman admiral, who sent a deputy; real power passed to local aghas and tax farmers, and revolts followed.
The muhassils of the Grand Vizier
Cyprus was granted to the Grand Vizier as a source of income and run by a muhassil who bought the right to collect its taxes, the arrangement that made both extortion and the Church's power possible.

en: Governor of the brief restored eyalet, remembered for good order and for beginning the aqueduct to Larnaca in 1747.
Muhassil who doubled the tax demand; Greeks and Turks together stormed the palace in Nicosia and killed him, one of the few joint risings of the period.
Muhassil who ordered the hanging of Archbishop Kyprianos and the beheading of the three bishops on 9 July 1821 and the executions and confiscations that followed.

After the Tanzimat reforms Cyprus was governed by a mutasarrif under the Archipelago province and then, from 1861 and again from 1870, as a separate mutasarrifate until the British took over the administration.
Archbishop under whom the Porte came to treat the prelates as spokesmen of the Orthodox flock, the step conventionally dated to 1660.
Consolidated the archbishop's standing as head of the Greek community, with the right to petition Constantinople over the governor's head.
Presided over the years when the archbishop and the four bishops collected the Christians' taxes and were, in practice, the island's civil government.
Interpreter to the governor and tax intermediary, the richest man on the island; executed at Constantinople in 1809 after complaints from both communities.
Founder of the Hellenic School of Nicosia in 1812; hanged from a tree outside the palace on 9 July 1821 in the reprisals for the Greek revolt.

Britain took over the administration in 1878 under the Cyprus Convention, keeping the island as a base on the road to India and Suez. It annexed Cyprus in 1914 and made it a Crown Colony in 1925. Roads, schools and courts were built and the population doubled, but the Greek majority's demand for union with Greece grew louder, exploding in the riots of 1931 and the armed EOKA campaign of 1955–59, which ended in independence rather than union.
First High Commissioner, who landed at Larnaca in July 1878 and set up the administration.
Governor whose Government House was burned in the October 1931 riots.
Governor of the authoritarian 'Palmerocracy' after 1931, with the legislature abolished.
Governor during the EOKA emergency; exiled Archbishop Makarios to the Seychelles in 1956.

en: Last Governor, who handed over power at independence on 16 August 1960.
Raised the British flag at Nicosia on 12 July 1878 and held the administration for ten days.
Built the first roads, courts and schools and the summer residence on the Troodos; the longest-serving of the early administrators.
Presided over the first stirrings of organised enosis politics in the Legislative Council.
High Commissioner during years of locust campaigns, agricultural debt and emigration.
Faced deadlock in the Legislative Council between Greek and Turkish members and the British bloc.
Opened the Cyprus Government Railway in 1905 and the rebuilt harbour at Famagusta.
In office when Britain annexed Cyprus in November 1914 after the Ottoman entry into the war.
Administered the island through the war, when Britain offered Cyprus to Greece and Athens declined.
Last High Commissioner and first Governor when Cyprus became a Crown Colony in 1925.
Held the governorship for a year in the immediate repression after the riots.
Relaxed some of Palmer's restrictions as war began and raised the Cyprus Regiment.
Governor through the war years, when trade unions and communal politics revived.
Offered a Consultative Assembly and a constitution which the Greek Cypriot leadership boycotted; resigned when the offer failed.
In office for the 1950 enosis plebiscite and the election of Makarios III as archbishop.
Governor when the constitution was again refused and EOKA opened its campaign on 1 April 1955.

Cyprus became independent on 16 August 1960 with Archbishop Makarios III as president and a power-sharing constitution guaranteed by Greece, Turkey and Britain, which kept two Sovereign Base Areas. The constitution broke down in 1963, United Nations peacekeepers arrived in 1964, and in 1974 a coup backed by the Greek junta was answered by a Turkish invasion that has divided the island since. The Republic joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2008; talks on reunification continue.
Archbishop and first president; survived the 1974 coup and returned to office until his death.
President through the aftermath of division and the 1983 declaration in the north.
Businessman-president who applied for European Community membership in 1990.
Veteran negotiator who led accession talks with the European Union.
President when Cyprus joined the EU; opposed the Annan reunification plan in the 2004 referendum.
Communist-party president; the euro was adopted and the 2012–13 banking crisis struck.
Steered the bailout and recovery; the Crans-Montana talks of 2017 ended without agreement.
Former foreign minister, elected president in February 2023.

en: Almost everything the first farmers lived on came by boat: emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils and pulses as seed grain, and sheep, goats, cattle and dogs as breeding stock, with Mesopotamian fallow deer released to be hunted rather than herded. Cattle failed and died out during the period and were not seen on the island again for some three thousand years, so meat came from deer, sheep, goats and pigs, while olives, figs, pistachios, plums and pears were gathered wild. There was no metal and no pottery; the only imports that survive are blades of Anatolian obsidian, about three hundred of them at Shillourokambos alone, and vessels were carved instead from hard grey andesite.

en: The language of these people is unrecoverable. Writing would not be invented anywhere for another five thousand years and no later text preserves a word of what was spoken here, so the most that can be said is that the settlers came from the Levant and Anatolia and are likely to have spoken something related to the pre-Semitic and pre-Indo-European languages of the Near East. It has occasionally been suggested that the non-Greek Eteocypriot still spoken at Amathus in the fourth century BCE descends from this earliest layer, but the suggestion is untestable and most scholars will not press it back beyond the Bronze Age.

en: There are no temples, no shrines and no unambiguous cult buildings; ritual, so far as it can be seen at all, happened in and under the house. At Khirokitia the dead were laid in shallow pits beneath the plastered floors with the knees drawn up, and a quern or another heavy stone was often placed on the body, adults and children alike, before a new floor was laid over them. Schematic stone heads and figurines were carved, and at Shillourokambos a man was buried with a cat laid beside him, but what any of it meant is guesswork.

en: Villages were small and tightly packed: Khirokitia, the largest known, is thought never to have held more than three hundred to six hundred people at a time in round stone houses inside a perimeter wall, and Klimonas, almost two thousand years older, had a communal round building ten metres across. The Khirokitia skeletons give a mean age at death of about thirty-five for men and thirty-three for women among those who survived childhood, with very high infant mortality, and men stood around 160 centimetres, women around 150. Diet was overwhelmingly terrestrial, with little or no marine food in the isotope record even at coastal sites, and the whole population descends from a deliberate seaborne migration that must have moved people, seed and livestock in organised boatloads.
